`abandoned` row conservative, and a final row complete; a trigger refuses any UPDATE of a `settled` or `abandoned` row and any change
to the identity and the reserved figures of an open one, and refuses DELETE (PostgreSQL also TRUNCATE, and revokes both from
`PUBLIC`).

**Migration and rollout.** `0133` only adds the table and its guards (nothing else references it and nothing reads it before the code
that writes it). Run it before the new code serves: a process on the new code with no table refuses a governed step with
`governed agent step token reservation refused: store_failed` and never calls its adapter. Rolling back the code leaves the table
unread; downgrading the migration drops the table and loses the charges counted against runs, so never do it where they matter.

| the step | result | recover by |
| --- | --- | --- |
| would take the run past its budget | `token_budget_exhausted`, nothing reserved, adapter not called | a larger `CALIBER_AGENT_RUN_MAX_TOKENS` (a new run: a finished run's budget is its own) |
| runs again on an attempt that holds a reservation (a node retry in the same process, or a process-level re-execution) | `reservation_replayed`, adapter not called | a node retry is the next attempt and reserves afresh; after a crash the attempt counter restarts at 1, so the resumed governed node is refused and the run fails: start a new run (see the known limit below) |
| the store cannot reserve | `store_failed`, adapter not called | the database; nothing was reserved |
| the worker died or was cancelled mid-call | the reservation stays `reserved`, counted in full, then `abandoned` after the grace | nothing: it is already charged; see the [recovery runbook](m-65-recovery-runbook.md#a-governed-step-refused-for-its-token-budget-or-left-a-reservation-open) |

**Known limit: crash recovery of a governed step is terminal (follow-up #1073).** The attempt counter (`_STEP_ATTEMPT`) restarts at 1 on every
process-level re-execution of a run. After a crash between the reservation and the settlement (or between the settlement and the
recording of the proposal) the resumed governed node reaches the same `(run, node, occurrence, attempt)`, finds the reservation, and is
refused with `reservation_replayed`: the run fails and only a new run proceeds. That fails closed and avoids a second provider spend
under one reservation, but it means a governed step cannot be resumed after a crash. The follow-up is to persist or derive the attempt so
a legitimate resume reuses or supersedes the open reservation safely.

Deleting a workflow whose runs hold reservations is refused with `409` (`cannot delete workflow: its runs have step token
reservations`), like run manifests and effect proposals.

Reading it back: `caliber.budget.step_reservation.run_token_usage(session_factory, run_id)` returns what a run has counted and how many
reservations are open and final. No route lists reservations yet.

**For the conformance suite (#769).** `reserve_step_tokens(session_factory, request, run_budget_tokens=...)` returns a
`StepReservation` (`created`, `state`, `reserved_tokens`, `charged_tokens`, `charge_basis`) or raises `ReservationRefused` whose `code`
is one of `token_budget_exhausted`, `reservation_replayed`, `request_invalid`, `budget_invalid`, `run_not_found`,
`reservation_mismatch`; `settle_step_tokens(session_factory, reservation, result)` returns the final row; `charge_for(reserved, result)`
is the pure rule; `abandon_stale(session_factory, lease, grace_seconds=...)` is the owner janitor. The scenario
`tests/egi_scenarios/test_v08_timeout_retry.py::test_budget_refuses_before_call` and the PostgreSQL races in
`tests/egi_scenarios/test_b08_token_reservation.py` are the oracle; `tests/conformance/test_agent_adapter_governed_plan.py` runs each
provider adapter through the reservation (charged as reported for honest usage, the whole reservation for every other result, no second
provider call on a replay).

## Adapter conformance suite: the rules every provider adapter passes (B08.5, #769)

The governed agent step has one boundary ([`run_agent_step`](#agent-step-adapters-the-boundary-every-provider-answers-through-b081b-720)) and
four provider adapters behind it. The conformance suite is the evidence that an adapter holds its side of that boundary, and it is
the same suite for every adapter: the four that ship (OpenAI chat completions, OpenAI Responses, the OpenAI Agents SDK and Anthropic
Messages) and any adapter written elsewhere. It adds no route, table, setting or migration; it calls no provider, reads no real clock
and needs no provider SDK.

Two modules ship with the package (`caliber.testing`, test support like the fault barriers) so that an adapter outside this repository
can run what the repository runs:

- `caliber.testing.agent_step_conformance`: the per-scenario harness that B08.1b introduced (moved here from `tests/`, which
  re-exports it), with its protected-tool canaries, fixed clock and `StepContext`;
- `caliber.testing.adapter_conformance`: the rules, the provider script language, `AdapterUnderTest`, and the report.

**Run it for the shipped adapters.** The real executor classes over canned transports, every rule, offline:

```text
cd caliber && pytest tests/conformance/test_agent_adapter_conformance.py     # 4 adapters x 41 rules
pytest tests/conformance/test_suite_fails_against_broken_adapters.py         # the suite fails when an adapter is broken
pytest tests/conformance/test_agent_adapter_governed_plan.py                 # the same adapters under the interpreter
pytest tests/conformance/test_agent_adapter_openai_agents_real_sdk.py        # the Agents adapter on the installed SDK
```

**Run it for your adapter.** An adapter is any object with `run_step(request, step_input) -> AgentStepResult`
(`AgentStepAdapter`). The suite needs one function from you, `build(script, probe)`: it returns a *fresh* adapter whose provider
transport plays `script`, an ordered list of what your provider does on its first, second, ... call (`Reply`, `Fault`, `Garbage`).
The transport calls `probe.provider_called(tools=[...], sent="...")` each time the provider would be called (`tools`, the names the
request offers the model, and `sent`, the request's text, are optional; the rules `offered_tools_are_the_agents_own` and
`read_tool_failure_is_class_only` are reported unsupported without them), and the adapter reads time from `probe.clock` (the fake the
rules move; an adapter that reads the real clock cannot be tested for a deadline). Something your transport cannot express raises
`Unsupported(reason)`: that passes for a rule marked optional (`invalid_argument_text`, `read_tool_failure_is_class_only`, `offered_tools_are_the_agents_own`) and fails for every other.

The complete example below is a correct adapter for a made-up provider and the `build` that stages the suite's scripts on it. It is
the file `tests/conformance/toy_adapter.py`, which `tests/conformance/test_example_third_party_adapter.py` runs exactly as the last
lines of the example say, and checks that the code quoted here is the file's. Every rule passes against it.

```python
from __future__ import annotations

import asyncio
import json
import logging
from collections.abc import Callable, Mapping
from dataclasses import dataclass
from datetime import datetime
from typing import Any

from caliber.contracts.agent_step import (
    AgentStepRequest,
    AgentStepResult,
    StepUsage,
)
from caliber.contracts.registry import ContractValidationError
from caliber.effects.records import ProposalError
from caliber.testing.adapter_conformance import (
    MALFORMED_USAGE,
    AdapterUnderTest,
    Call,
    Fault,
    Garbage,
    ProviderProbe,
    ProviderUsage,
    Reply,
    Script,
    fault_exception,
)
from caliber.workflows.agent_step import (
    ADAPTER_TIMEOUT,
    MALFORMED_RESULT,
    PROVIDER_ERROR,
    AgentStepInput,
    StepDeadlineReached,
    StepToolBudgetExceeded,
    answer,
    failure,
    proposal_from_call,
)

logger = logging.getLogger("acme_adapter")



class _Unreadable(Exception):  # noqa: N818 - what the provider sent cannot be read; never carries its text
    pass


@dataclass
class _Tally:
    prompt: int = 0
    completion: int = 0
    turns: int = 0
    tool_calls: int = 0
    estimated: bool = False

    def usage(self) -> StepUsage:
        total = self.prompt + self.completion
        return StepUsage(self.prompt, self.completion, total, self.turns, self.tool_calls)

    @property
    def source(self) -> str:
        return "estimated" if self.estimated else "provider"


def _count(value: object) -> int:
    if type(value) is not int or not 0 <= value <= 2_147_483_647:
        raise _Unreadable
    return value


class ToyAdapter:
    """One governed step against a provider callable; the example every rule of the conformance suite is run on."""

    def __init__(
        self,
        provider: Callable[[list[dict[str, Any]], list[str]], Any],
        *,
        now: Callable[[], datetime],
    ):
        self._provider = provider
        self._now = now

    def run_step(  # noqa: PLR0911, PLR0912 - one loop, one exit per way a step can end
        self, request: AgentStepRequest, step_input: AgentStepInput
    ) -> AgentStepResult:
        tally = _Tally()
        read_tools = dict(step_input.read_tools)
        messages = [*step_input.history, {"role": "user", "content": step_input.input_text}]
        while True:
            if (limit := self._limit_reached(request, tally)) is not None:
                return self._stop(request, limit, tally)
            try:
                reply = self._call_provider(messages, sorted(read_tools))
            except (TimeoutError, asyncio.TimeoutError):
                return failure(request, ADAPTER_TIMEOUT)
            except Exception as exc:
                return self._provider_failed(request, exc)
            try:
                calls = self._read_reply(reply, tally, step_input)
                if reply.get("finish") == "length" or self._over_budget(request, tally):
                    return self._stop(request, "max_tokens", tally)
                protected = [call for call in calls if call["name"] not in read_tools]
                if protected:
                    return self._propose(request, protected[0], tally, step_input)
                if not calls:
                    return answer(
                        request, "completed", usage=tally.usage(), usage_source=tally.source
                    )
                for call in calls:
                    if self._tool_limit_reached(request, tally):
                        return self._stop(request, "max_tool_calls", tally)
                    tally.tool_calls += 1
                    try:
                        result = self._run_read_tool(read_tools[call["name"]], call["arguments"])
                    except StepToolBudgetExceeded:
                        return self._stop(request, "max_tool_calls", tally)
                    except StepDeadlineReached:
                        return self._stop(request, "deadline", tally)
                    except Exception as exc:
                        # The model is told which kind of failure it was; the message is the tool's, not the model's.
                        result = json.dumps({"_error": type(exc).__name__})
                    messages.append({"role": "tool", "content": str(result)})
            except _Unreadable:
                return failure(request, MALFORMED_RESULT)

    @staticmethod
    def _stop(request: AgentStepRequest, reason: str, tally: _Tally) -> AgentStepResult:
        return answer(request, reason, usage=tally.usage(), usage_source=tally.source)

    def _limit_reached(self, request: AgentStepRequest, tally: _Tally) -> str | None:
        """A limit that forbids another provider call: turns, tokens, then the deadline."""
        limits = request.limits
        if tally.turns >= limits.max_turns:
            return "max_turns"
        if tally.prompt + tally.completion >= limits.max_tokens:
            return "max_tokens"
        if self._now() >= limits.deadline_at:
            return "deadline"
        return None

    @staticmethod
    def _over_budget(request: AgentStepRequest, tally: _Tally) -> bool:
        """The response just read took the step past ``max_tokens``: whatever it asked for is not acted on."""
        return tally.prompt + tally.completion > request.limits.max_tokens

    @staticmethod
    def _tool_limit_reached(request: AgentStepRequest, tally: _Tally) -> bool:
        return tally.tool_calls >= request.limits.max_tool_calls

    def _call_provider(self, messages: list[dict[str, Any]], tools: list[str]) -> Any:
        return self._provider(messages, tools)

    @staticmethod
    def _provider_failed(request: AgentStepRequest, exc: Exception) -> AgentStepResult:
        # Only the exception's class is logged: its text is the provider's, and may quote the prompt.
        logger.warning("provider call failed (%s)", type(exc).__name__)
        return failure(request, PROVIDER_ERROR)

    @staticmethod
    def _run_read_tool(tool: Callable[..., Any], arguments: dict[str, Any]) -> Any:
        return tool(**arguments)

    def _read_reply(
        self, reply: Any, tally: _Tally, step_input: AgentStepInput
    ) -> list[dict[str, Any]]:
        """The reply's tool calls (name and decoded arguments); its usage is added to ``tally``."""
        if not isinstance(reply, Mapping):
            raise _Unreadable
        usage = reply.get("usage")
        if usage is None:
            tally.estimated = True
            tally.prompt += len(step_input.input_text.split())
            tally.completion += len(str(reply.get("text") or "").split())
        elif isinstance(usage, Mapping):
            tally.prompt += _count(usage.get("prompt"))
            tally.completion += _count(usage.get("completion"))
        else:
            raise _Unreadable
        tally.turns += 1
        names = {binding.local_name for binding in step_input.agent.tools}
        calls = []
        try:
            for raw in reply.get("tool_calls") or []:
                text = raw["arguments"]
                arguments = json.loads(text) if isinstance(text, str) else text
                if not isinstance(arguments, dict) or raw["name"] not in names:
                    raise _Unreadable
                calls.append({"name": raw["name"], "arguments": arguments})
        except (KeyError, TypeError, ValueError):
            raise _Unreadable from None
        return calls

    def _propose(
        self,
        request: AgentStepRequest,
        call: dict[str, Any],
        tally: _Tally,
        step_input: AgentStepInput,
    ) -> AgentStepResult:
        """The model's protected call as one unbound proposal that names the function it called, and claims nothing."""
        del step_input
        try:
            action = proposal_from_call(call["name"], call["arguments"])
        except (ProposalError, ContractValidationError, TypeError, ValueError):
            raise _Unreadable from None
        return answer(
            request,
            "proposed_action",
            usage=tally.usage(),
            proposed_actions=(action,),
            usage_source=tally.source,
        )

def toy_provider(
    script: Script, probe: ProviderProbe
) -> Callable[[list[dict[str, Any]], list[str]], Any]:
    """The made-up provider the suite's scripts are played on."""
    remaining = list(script)

    def provider(messages: list[dict[str, Any]], tools: list[str]) -> Any:
        probe.provider_called(tools=tools, sent=json.dumps(messages, default=str))
        if not remaining:
            raise RuntimeError("the script has no reply left")
        item = remaining.pop(0)
        if isinstance(item, Fault):
            raise TimeoutError(item.text) if item.kind == "timeout" else fault_exception(item)
        if isinstance(item, Garbage):
            return ["not", "a", "reply", item.text]
        return _wire(item)

    return provider


def _wire(reply: Reply) -> dict[str, Any]:
    wire: dict[str, Any] = {
        "text": reply.text,
        "tool_calls": [_wire_call(call) for call in reply.calls],
        "finish": "length" if reply.cut_off else "stop",
    }
    if reply.usage is MALFORMED_USAGE:
        wire["usage"] = {"prompt": "many", "completion": "some"}
    elif isinstance(reply.usage, ProviderUsage):
        wire["usage"] = {"prompt": reply.usage.prompt, "completion": reply.usage.completion}
    return wire


def _wire_call(call: Call) -> dict[str, Any]:
    text = call.arguments if isinstance(call.arguments, str) else json.dumps(call.arguments)
    return {"name": call.name, "arguments": text}


def toy_subject() -> AdapterUnderTest:
    """The conformance subject for :class:`ToyAdapter`: ``build`` returns a fresh adapter over a provider playing the script."""
    return AdapterUnderTest(
        name="toy",
        build=lambda script, probe: ToyAdapter(toy_provider(script, probe), now=probe.clock.now),
    )


import pytest

from caliber.testing.adapter_conformance import RULES, check_rule, conformance_report

SUBJECT = toy_subject()  # for your adapter: AdapterUnderTest(name="acme", build=your_build)


@pytest.mark.parametrize("rule", RULES, ids=lambda rule: rule.id)
def test_acme_conforms(rule):
    check_rule(SUBJECT, rule.id)  # raises ConformanceFailure naming the adapter, the rule and what was seen


print(conformance_report(SUBJECT).render())  # one table: PASS / FAIL / UNSUPPORTED per rule, then a verdict
```

**What every run checks, whatever the rule.** A rule plays its script twice: through the platform's entry (`run_agent_step`) and
by calling the adapter alone on a fresh copy, because an adapter may not rely on the boundary to catch its mistakes. Both runs must
satisfy: the result is a schema-valid `agent_step_result` that answers the asked step; **no protected tool ran** (a canary sits behind
the protected tool's binding and in the unfiltered tool registry); the provider payload planted in the script (`SECRET_MARKER`) is in no
result, log record (every logger, every level, `extra=` fields included), warning, stdout or stderr; and the adapter returned a typed
result instead of raising. (The nine rules that come from the per-scenario harness, from `completes` to `claims_commit`, check the
result, the canaries and the log records, which is what that harness has always checked.) Log capture cannot see a logger created during
the run that turns propagation off, or output that bypasses `logging`, `warnings` and the standard streams.

| Rule | What it demands |
| --- | --- |
| `completes` | A final answer completes the step and reports exactly the provider's usage |
| `read_tool_call` | A read tool the model calls runs through read_tools, and usage sums over turns |
| `proposes_protected_tool` | A protected tool call is one unbound proposal that names the called function, never executed |
| `model_lies_about_effect_class` | An effect class the model volunteers is refused (malformed_result), never proposed |
| `budget_exhausted` | A response the provider cut off is a limit stop that keeps the provider's usage |
| `provider_error` | A provider error is a typed error result carrying no provider text |
| `provider_timeout` | A provider timeout is adapter_timeout |
| `unreadable_output` | Output the adapter cannot read is malformed_result |
| `claims_commit` | Output that claims an effect happened is malformed_result, never a proposal |
| `hostile_model_text` | Hostile model text is inert: nothing is carried into the result, a log or a tool |
| `extra_fields_rejected` | A proposal that carries a field the contract does not have is malformed, never a proposal |
| `oversized_arguments_refused` | Proposal arguments larger than the intent's limit are malformed, never recorded |
| `deep_arguments_refused` | Proposal arguments nested deeper than the intent's limit are malformed |
| `lone_surrogate_refused` | A lone surrogate in a proposal is malformed: it cannot be canonicalised or stored |
| `invalid_argument_text` | Tool arguments that are not a JSON object are malformed for a proposal, and never crash the adapter |
| `unknown_tool_not_run` | A tool the agent does not have is never run, and the step is not completed |
| `connector_version_claim` | A connector, version or class the model volunteers is refused (malformed_result), never carried into a proposal |
| `proposal_names_the_called_tool` | A protected tool's call (its arguments only) is a proposal that carries the called function's name and no claim |
| `read_tools_authoritative` | Only the callables the platform classified read are run, whatever the binding says |
| `one_proposed_action` | Two protected calls in one response are at most one proposal, and the second never runs |
| `proposal_ends_step` | A proposal ends the step: the provider is not asked again after it |
| `handoff_not_followed` | A governed step never follows a handoff: the target's tools are not run |
| `read_tool_failure_is_class_only` | A read tool that raises never crashes the adapter, and its message is not handed to the provider |
| `offered_tools_are_the_agents_own` | The model is offered only tools the agent has: no handoff, no target's tool |
| `invalid_request_refused` | A request that is not a valid step, or not for this agent, never reaches the adapter |
| `limits_before_work` | A step with no turn, no token or no time left never reaches the adapter or its provider |
| `turn_limit` | The adapter asks the provider for no more turns than the limit, and a stopped step proposes nothing |
| `tool_call_limit` | No read tool runs past max_tool_calls, and the step stops instead of going on |
| `token_limit` | A step over max_tokens stops with the provider's usage kept and proposes nothing |
| `deadline_limit` | A step past its deadline asks for nothing more, runs no tool and proposes nothing |
| `adapter_cannot_raise_limits` | The platform holds a step to the limits it set, whatever the adapter was told |
| `honest_usage_is_charged_as_reported` | Usage the provider reported is reported as the provider's, so it is charged as spent |
| `missing_usage_not_fabricated` | A response without usage is reported estimated or unknown, never as genuine figures |
| `malformed_usage_charged_whole` | Unreadable usage never lowers the charge, and no proposal rides on it |
| `asyncio_timeout_is_adapter_timeout` | A timeout raised by asyncio itself is adapter_timeout, on every supported Python |
| `no_hidden_retry` | A failed provider call is not retried: the provider is called once, and the retry is the platform's |
| `cancellation_propagates` | Cancellation and interruption reach the caller, so the reservation stays open (the call may have spent) |
| `errors_are_payload_free` | A failure is a fixed code: no provider text, argument or tool name reaches a result or any output |
| `deterministic` | The same step against the same provider answers identically, proposals included |
| `fresh_state_per_step` | An adapter carries nothing from one step to the next: each answers its own request |
| `input_isolation` | The adapter gets its own copy of the request and its tools, and changes none of what it was handed |

**The platform enforces some of this whatever an adapter does**, and the suite says so rather than pretend otherwise. The limits are
held by the boundary (`before_work_stop`, the tool meter, `_enforce_limits`): an adapter that overruns still has its proposal dropped and
the typed stop returned. What an adapter alone decides is what it *spends*: whether it stops asking the provider once a limit is
reached. A rule therefore asserts both: the result through the platform and the adapter's own answer when called alone, and the
provider calls it made. `adapter_cannot_raise_limits` is the one limit rule with no "alone" half: its point is that the boundary holds
an adapter to the limits it set although the adapter was told otherwise.

**A subject may declare the stops it cannot make.** `AdapterUnderTest(unbounded_in_loop=...)`, from `proposal`, `tool_calls`, `tokens` and
`deadline`, is for an adapter whose SDK offers no hook between provider calls for that stop: the rules then do not demand the adapter's own
stop (the spend past the limit is bounded by the token reservation only). The declaration is the subject's own, so it is public: the report
prints it on its second line (`cannot stop asking the provider at: ...`), and it is read in the pull request or the CI log like any other
line of the report. It relaxes only those spend checks, never a rule. **No shipped adapter declares any.** The OpenAI Agents SDK takes
`max_turns` for the run and `tool_use_behavior` (a function; present since `openai-agents` 0.0.7 and run here on 0.20 and 0.24, where the SDK requires the
function to return its own `ToolsToFinalOutputResult`, which the adapter uses) for everything else: after each turn's tools the adapter's function ends the run for a proposal, the tool-call limit, the token budget
or the deadline, before the model is asked again. `test_agent_adapter_openai_agents_real_sdk.py` runs that on the installed SDK with a scripted
model, so the emulation the conformance suite uses cannot drift from what the SDK does. (Separately and before this change: the adapter
already builds `FunctionTool(needs_approval=..., timeout_seconds=...)`, which `openai-agents` 0.0.7 does not accept, so the declared
minimum `>=0.0.7` is stale for the adapter as a whole; follow-up.)

**The suite has been shown to fail.** `tests/conformance/broken_adapters.py` holds 39 deliberately broken adapters, each the reference
adapter with exactly one defect (it runs a protected tool, strips a claimed `receipt_id` and proposes anyway, forgets usage on a cut-off,
fabricates figures for a response without usage, retries a provider call, swallows a cancellation, misses an asyncio timeout, logs the
model's text or the provider's exception, hands a tool's exception message to the provider, offers a handoff target, ignores a limit,
carries the first step's result into the second, rewrites the limits of the request it was handed), and
`test_suite_fails_against_broken_adapters.py` requires that each fails the rule written for it for a reason the rule states, and that the
intact adapter passes all 41. The rules the boundary decides (`limits_before_work`, `adapter_cannot_raise_limits`,
`invalid_request_refused` and the copy half of `input_isolation`) are shown to fail against a boundary with that enforcement removed.

**Inside a governed plan** (`test_agent_adapter_governed_plan.py`, SQLite, the real interpreter and reservation ledger): for each shipped
adapter, a protected call is one recorded proposal charged as reported with the protected tool's mutation counter at zero; a lying effect
class records nothing; a provider error, a timeout, unreadable, missing or malformed usage, and a claimed commit are each charged the
whole reservation (`conservative`) and carry no provider text into the run error or the log; a replayed step is refused with
`reservation_replayed` and its provider is not reached again; a step past the run's budget never reaches the provider; a timed-out
attempt keeps its reservation, and its retry is reserved again and calls the provider once; a cancelled step leaves its reservation open
and counted in full; and a governed agent with a handoff is refused before any adapter runs.

A failure reads like this (a reference adapter that retries a failed provider call; 3 of its 41 rules failed). The output
is what the suite prints, and `test_example_third_party_adapter.py` runs it again and requires these lines:

```text
adapter conformance: RetriesTheProviderOnce
  FAIL        provider_timeout                     scenario provider_timeout: expected adapter_timeout, got provider_error
  FAIL        asyncio_timeout_is_adapter_timeout   an asyncio timeout (through the platform): expected an error with no proposal, got completed with 0 proposed
  FAIL        no_hidden_retry                      an error (through the platform): expected an error with no proposal, got completed with 0 proposed
DOES NOT CONFORM (3 failed)
```

**Findings the suite produced, and what was done.**

- The OpenAI Agents adapter read a read tool the platform refused for the deadline (`StepDeadlineReached`) as a tool failure, so a step
  that ran past its deadline ended `error` / `malformed_result` instead of `deadline`. It no longer does.
- The OpenAI Agents adapter let the SDK ask the model again after a proposal, a refused tool, a spent budget or a passed deadline, because
  it chose `tool_use_behavior="run_llm_again"`; the extra model calls were bounded only by the reservation. It now passes a function that
  ends the run at those points (an earlier version of this section called the SDK unable to do that: wrong, the SDK has the hook).
- The chat and Responses adapters handed a failing read tool's exception message (`Type: message`) to the provider as the tool result;
  the Agents and Anthropic adapters sent the class name only. The governed paths of the chat and Responses adapters now send the class
  name only (`_execute_model_tool_call(..., error_detail=False)`); the ungoverned loops are unchanged.
- The Anthropic adapter recognised only the builtin `TimeoutError`; on Python 3.10, where `asyncio.TimeoutError` is a different class, an
  asyncio timeout became `provider_error` instead of `adapter_timeout`. It now recognises both, and a rule (`asyncio_timeout_is_adapter_timeout`)
  raises a real `asyncio.wait_for` timeout at every adapter.
- The harness' direct call of the adapter was not checked for logs; it is now.

**Not covered, so not claimed.** The suite proves an adapter's behaviour over its stub of the provider, not the provider's: it cannot show
that a real client is configured as its stub is, that a provider's tokens are what it reported, or that a model cannot be talked into a
harmful proposal (a proposal is only ever the model's claim, which the platform binds and an approver reads). `another_steps_result`
(a provider that answers another step's identity) cannot be staged through a provider script and stays in the per-scenario harness. The
Agents and Anthropic adapters and the boundary emit no spans; the chat and Responses adapters run a read tool through a shared helper
that opens a tool span carrying the model's arguments and the tool's output (the ungoverned loops do too), and no span is checked: the
checked outputs are the result, log records, warnings, stdout and stderr. A read tool that raises ends an Agents step `malformed_result` but
lets the other adapters' model recover: both are allowed (the rule requires only that the message is not handed to the provider and that
nothing crashes), and the Agents policy is pinned by its own test. `FakeWorkflowExecutor` is the platform's scripted adapter (its entries
are structured, so a hostile model cannot be staged through it) and has its own tests (`tests/test_agent_step_adapter.py`); the suite
covers the four provider adapters, not five. Run it without `python -O`: the harness uses `assert` and the suite refuses to run
without them.

## Policy decisions

`caliber.policy.decisions.decide(...)` (B03.3, #671; migration `0117`, table `caliber_policy_decisions`) answers "may
this run do this action on this resource, for this purpose, right now?" with a typed `PolicyDecision` and records it,
allow or deny, immutably (ADR 0003 `policy_decision` v1 plus the run, subject and workload it was asked about; there
are no foreign keys, so a decision about a grant that does not exist is still evidence).

- **Exact identity, no fallback.** The caller supplies `run_id`, `grant_id`, the `Subject` and the `Workload`. A
  different run, an unknown grant, another subject (user, authentication method or project) and another workload each
  deny, and nothing is looked up by recency.
- **One reason, a fixed order:** `grant_not_found`, `subject_mismatch`, `workload_mismatch`, `grant_revoked`,
  `grant_expired`, `not_a_member`, `action_not_allowed`, `role_not_allowed`, `resource_not_allowed` (the
  [run grant](#run-grants) checks, including the current membership and role), then the policy's own:
  `policy_version_mismatch` (the grant was issued under another policy version), `purpose_not_allowed`,
  `explicit_deny`, `unknown_action_risk` and `risk_above_ceiling`. An unavailable store is `authority_unavailable`.
  An allow carries no reason codes.
- **Explicit maps, never ordering.** Each action has an explicit risk number in the policy (every action in
  `resource_access.PROJECT_ACTIONS` must have one; a test fails otherwise), compared with the policy's ceiling.
  `policy-v1` has a ceiling of 4 (risk equal to the ceiling is allowed). Risk 5 means "a person, never a run": project
  administration (archive, restore, members, ownership transfer) and every approval or acceptance
  (`resource.approve`, `release.approve`, `release.quality_signoff`, `change_request.accept`), so no grant can make a
  run approve its own work (Beta keeps a human accountable owner and human protected-action approval, ADR 0004).
  Explicit denies are exact `(action, resource)` pairs. A `Policy` is read-only and type-checked.
- **Replayable.** `input_hash` is the SHA-256 of the canonical JSON of every input (run, grant, subject, workload,
  action, resource, purpose and the live scopes) plus the policy's own digest; the clock is not an input. The same inputs under the same policy hash identically.
- **Transactions.** A decision is flushed, never committed. For initial admission the run, its grant and the decision
  share one uncommitted transaction and the caller commits only after an allow; a denial rolls all of it back. If an
  decision cannot be recorded, the answer is a deny with `persisted = False` (an allow becomes
  `authority_unavailable`; a deny keeps its reason and gains `authority_unavailable`), and
  `PolicyDecision.allowed` is true only for a recorded allow. A decision never touches the run manifest. The record
  is written in a savepoint, so a failed record never poisons the caller's transaction. **Consumers must know:** a
  denied initial admission rolls its decision row back with the transaction, so evidence of a *denial* must be
  written separately (the audit record of B03.5, or a decision made in its own transaction), and on SQLite
  (development only) a savepoint that is the first write of a transaction commits it, so call `decide` after the
  run and grant writes.
- **Callers must not leak identity mismatches.** `decide` records the specific reason (`subject_mismatch` and
  `workload_mismatch` reveal that a grant exists). It is server-internal: any layer that answers a client (HTTP, the
  admission API) must collapse identity and grant-lookup failures into one uniform refusal. `purpose` is stored
  verbatim: it names why, never context or payload.
- **Malformed input is a bug, not a decision.** A blank, oversized or control-character id, action, resource or
  purpose, a naive `now`, or a non-`Subject` raises `DecisionInputError` and records nothing.
- **Immutable.** Triggers refuse `UPDATE` and `DELETE` (`TRUNCATE` too on PostgreSQL) and the ORM raises
  `ImmutableRecordError`; as with run manifests, run the application as a role without those privileges.
- **Audited (B03.5, #688).** Every recorded decision also writes one audit-log row through `audit.record`, in the
  decision's own savepoint, so the two exist together: `action` is `policy_allow` (severity `standard`) or
  `policy_deny` (severity `high`, or `standard` when every reason is ordinary lifecycle: `grant_expired`, `grant_revoked`, `not_a_member`), `actor` the subject, `entity_type` `policy_decision`, `entity_id` the decision id,
  and `details` the run, grant and workload ids, the action, resource and purpose, the result, the reason codes, the
  policy version and the input hash. The run's input, context and any secret are never in it (and the audit log's
  redactor runs over it anyway). If the decision and its audit row cannot be written (the store is down) the answer
  is an unrecorded deny (`authority_unavailable`) and one structured error log line carries the decision, run, grant,
  action and result; nothing is allowed that is not on record.
  At **initial admission** the decision's own rows are rolled back with the refused run (nothing about a refused run
  is stored), so the denial's audit row is written *afterwards* in its own short transaction from the decision's ids and
  reasons (`admission.record_denial`; a failure there is logged and never changes the refusal).

Recovery: `grant_*`, `not_a_member`, `role_not_allowed`, `action_not_allowed` and `resource_not_allowed` are as in the
grant table above; `policy_version_mismatch` means the run must be admitted again under the current policy;
`purpose_not_allowed` and `explicit_deny` are policy decisions to change deliberately, not retry; `risk_above_ceiling`
means the action cannot be done by a run (use the human-approval path or a person); `unknown_action_risk` means the
policy lacks a risk for the action and must be extended; `subject_mismatch` and `workload_mismatch` are always a bug
or an attack: fix the caller.

## Release evaluation: the evaluator executes queued attempts (B10.2, #707)

`POST /projects/{project_id}/releases/{release_id}/evaluate` queues one `caliber_workspace_release_evaluations` row
(`queued`) per attempt. `WorkspaceReleaseEvaluator` (`caliber/src/caliber/orchestrator/workspace_release_evaluator.py`)
is the owner-only loop that picks them up. It reuses the service's own queue and lease
(`claim_workspace_release_evaluation`); there is no second queue.

> It is still opt-in. With the feature and worker flags enabled, the evaluator claims a row, resolves the release's
> own immutable revision pins, runs the configured EvalProvider, and completes the attempt. If the lease expires,
> the next owner records the abandoned attempt and claims a new fenced attempt; provider run identifiers observed
> before a crash remain attached to the evaluation and are deduplicated.

- **One claim per tick, oldest first.** Every `CALIBER_WORKSPACE_RELEASE_EVALUATOR_INTERVAL_SECONDS` (default 5, from 0.5
  to 3600) it claims the `queued` row with the oldest `requested_at` (ties by id). The row becomes `running` with
  `started_by`, `started_at`, `heartbeat_at` and a lease of `CALIBER_WORKSPACE_RELEASE_EVALUATOR_LEASE_SECONDS` (default
  300, from 1 to 86400; inf and nan are refused when the settings load). A row that is not `queued` (running under
  another claimer, `succeeded`, `failed`) is never touched. `GET .../evaluations/{evaluation_id}` shows it.
- **The claim identity.** `claimed_by` (and `started_by`) hold `workspace-release-evaluator-<pid>-<id>`, followed by
  `:t<token>` when the claim was fenced (the fencing token of the execution-owner lease it was made under; no suffix
  outside the reference profile). That is how the token is kept without a migration: an attempt claimed by owner 1 reads
  `...:t1`, one claimed after a takeover `...:t2`. The evaluator passes this identity and the attempt number to the
  service's heartbeat and complete calls (it is the `worker_id` of `ClaimedEvaluation`), and may read the token back
  from the row.
- **Pinned execution.** Before the provider call the worker loads only the release's `revision_id` and its
  `CaliberWorkspaceRevisionResource` rows. It requires one `candidate`, one `evaluation` dataset, and one `evaluation`
  judge pin; optional `baseline` pins are also revision-local. Each registered adapter resolves and snapshots its
  exact resource again, and a changed resource digest, missing adapter, missing pin, provider mismatch, or digest
  mismatch blocks the release without calling the provider. The request carries the exact dataset version and judge
  configuration; it never follows an unrelated workflow/run manifest or a mutable alias.
- **Result provenance and settlement.** The provider result records a SHA-256 evidence digest containing the plan and
  input digests, candidate/baseline scores, example count, thresholds, and `provider`/`simulated` provenance. A score
  below the pinned aggregate threshold becomes `no_go`; an unavailable plan/provider or invalid result becomes a
  retryable `blocked` outcome. Completion uses the same release lock version captured before provider work, so a
  concurrent transition cannot be overwritten.
- **Evidence-bound gate digest (B10.3, #714).** A provider must return one per-example result row for every pinned
  dataset example. The worker persists the canonical `gate_evidence` block on the evaluation attempt before settling the
  release. It contains the complete rows, a dataset digest derived from `example_id`/input/expected/weight/tags, the
  scored-result digest, per-scorer valid-row/weight denominators, candidate/baseline aggregates, thresholds and
  provider provenance. `evaluation_evidence_sha256` is the digest of that exact block and can be recomputed without a
  provider call. A missing row set or row-count mismatch blocks settlement and writes no gate evidence.
- **Durable attempt history and recovery (B10.4, #721).** The parent evaluation row remains the idempotent public
  queue/status record. Each claim also creates one row in `caliber_workspace_release_evaluation_attempts`, keyed by
  `(evaluation_id, attempt_number)`, with its worker identity, lease, status and provider run identifiers. When a
  lease expires, the old attempt becomes `orphaned` and the next claim increments the attempt number; the old row and
  any run identifiers are never overwritten. A provider run observed before settlement is recorded immediately, so a
  crash after an external call remains auditable. Completion, heartbeat and run-recording operations are fenced to
  the current attempt; a stale worker cannot settle the recovered release. Only the current attempt can become the
  authoritative completion, and all parent/provider run identifiers are merged without duplicates.
- **Matching successful gate evidence (B10.5, #732).** Manual quality/final decisions and automatic/break-glass
  release paths accept only a release-local evaluation row with `status=succeeded` whose canonical evidence recomputes
  to the release-bound digest and matches the evaluation's plan and input digests. The evidence must preserve provider
  and simulated/real provenance, satisfy the recorded aggregate criteria, and contain no critical-failure or waiver
  bypass. Missing, stale, tampered, non-passing, or out-of-scope evidence fails closed; break-glass does not waive a
  failed critical gate.
- **Adapter refusal (B10.6, #740).** A release operation that names a resource type with no registered adapter returns
  HTTP `409` with the stable payload `{"reason":"adapter_unavailable","adapter":"<resource type>","disabled_by":"profile"}`.
  Deployments that construct the registry from an environment-controlled feature may set `disabled_by` to that exact
  `CALIBER_*` variable instead. The refusal is emitted before an operation lock or durable operation is created, so the
  recovery is to enable/register the named adapter and retry the same intent; it is not evidence that an external effect
  was attempted. When the release-candidate feature itself is off, the existing route gate still returns HTTP `404`
  `reason_code=feature_disabled` and names `CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES`.
- **Owner-only and fenced.** It runs only in the process holding the execution-owner lease (see above), and in the
  reference profile each claim is made in a transaction that first runs `assert_fenced` with the exact lease the owner
  captured. A process whose lease was taken over, expired or cannot be checked claims nothing and records nothing; the
  log says `workspace release evaluator is no longer the execution owner (<reason>); nothing claimed`. On PostgreSQL
  the fenced claim sets `lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout` to a third of `CALIBER_EXECUTION_LEASE_SECONDS` (at least
  100 ms), the same bound the lease calls use. Two claimers racing for one row cannot both win
  (`FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` on PostgreSQL and a conditional `UPDATE ... WHERE status = 'queued'`); the loser claims
  nothing that tick and the next tick takes the next row.
- **Opt-in, and dormant while the feature is off.** The evaluator is built only when
  `CALIBER_FEATURE_RELEASE_CANDIDATES=true` *and* `CALIBER_WORKSPACE_RELEASE_EVALUATOR_ENABLED=true` (default **false**).
  Setting the second without the first logs a warning at startup and does nothing; with
  the feature off the release routes keep answering `404 feature_disabled`. When it does start it logs a WARNING that
  the worker is enabled and an INFO for each completed evaluation. `CALIBER_BACKGROUND_TASKS_ENABLED=false` stops it like
  every loop. A manually constructed worker without its provider and adapter registry is claim-only test/dry-run mode;
  the server always supplies both dependencies.
- **A clean stop gives the claims back.** On shutdown or when the lease is lost the controller stops the loops;
  `stop()` then marks this process's own still-`running` attempt history as `requeued` and sets the parent claim back
  to `queued`, clearing `claimed_by`, `started_by`, `started_at`, `heartbeat_at` and `lease_expires_at` in one
  compare-and-set statement on its own claim identity. It never touches a row another worker owns, and it works after
  the lease is gone. A crash, a kill or a stop that outlives `CALIBER_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_SECONDS` leaves the attempt
  `running` until the next owner observes the expired lease and records it as `orphaned`.
- **Liveness is write-only for now.** Every tick, idle ones included, writes a `caliber_worker_heartbeats` row of kind
  `workspace_release_evaluator`; a clean stop removes it and a replaced evaluator's stale row is reaped after a few
  poll intervals. Nothing reads that kind yet (`/readiness` queue health reads the `workflow_run` kind only), so it is a
  row an operator can query, not a probe.
- **No row content in logs or errors.** The log carries evaluation and release ids, the attempt number, the claim
  identity and the lease refusal reason, never the plan or input digests.

**Known limits.** An idle tick still writes a heartbeat row and runs one indexed `SELECT`. A tick still running when the
stop grace ends is abandoned (a thread cannot be cancelled) and can claim a row after the requeue. A queued row whose
claim keeps failing with an unexpected error is retried first on every tick, so it holds up the rows behind it.

**Inspecting recovered attempts** (a crashed or killed process, or an expired stop grace, left an attempt `running`).
The next owner recovers these automatically after `lease_expires_at` is in the past. Inspect both the parent queue row
and its immutable attempt history:

```sql
SELECT evaluation_id, workspace_release_id, claimed_by, lease_expires_at
FROM caliber_workspace_release_evaluations
WHERE status = 'running' AND claimed_by LIKE 'workspace-release-evaluator-%';

SELECT evaluation_id, attempt_number, worker_id, status, provider_run_ids, authoritative,
       completed_at, error_code
FROM caliber_workspace_release_evaluation_attempts
WHERE status IN ('running', 'orphaned', 'requeued')
ORDER BY evaluation_id, attempt_number;
```

**Rollback.** Unset `CALIBER_WORKSPACE_RELEASE_EVALUATOR_ENABLED` (or set it false) and restart: a clean stop of the old
process requeues its claims, and a new process claims nothing. If the old process did not stop cleanly, recover only
expired rows with the SQL above. There is no migration and nothing else to undo.
## Reserved tool names and refused paths (#641)

The protected-effect inventory (`docs/architecture/protected-effect-paths.md`) classifies a built-in tool by its
**name**, and the tool registry is unique only on (name, version). So a tool someone registers as `grep_files`
could be taken for the built-in. Registration therefore refuses every name a built-in owns, and the inventory
trusts a tool's name only when the tool really is CALIBER's own.

**Reserved names.** The sixteen tools CALIBER seeds: `read_text_file`, `list_folder_files`, `grep_files`,
`regex_search`, `grok_parse`, `sandbox_python`, `list_workdir_files`, `read_workdir_file`, `get_file_metadata`,
`write_workdir_file`, `create_artifact`, `extract_document`, `memory_search`, `memory_list`, `list_entities` and
`memory_add`. The comparison is stricter than the resolver's exact match: case and surrounding spaces are ignored, and so are a
`tool.` prefix and a `.vN` suffix, so `Grep_Files`, ` grep_files ` and `tool.grep_files.v2` are all reserved. A name
that merely contains one (`grep_files_v2`, `my_grep_files`) is free. The rule applies in every profile, to every
owner, module and version. The names of the trusted connectors (`document_request`, `document-request`, `http`, `registered_tool`, `openapi_http`, `openapi-http`, `mcp`, `mcp-tool`; see
[Trusted connector admission](#trusted-connector-admission-b123a-738)) are reserved the same way, with a message that names
the connector instead of a built-in tool.

**Where it is enforced.** `POST /tools`, `POST /openapi-integrations/{id}/tool-drafts/{draft_id}/publish` and the
Aria publisher (`AssistantPublisher`, for a tool draft). Nothing is written when a name is refused. CALIBER's own
seeding is unaffected.

```text
POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/tools   {"name": "grep_files", "version": "1.0", ...}
409 {"detail": "reserved_tool_name: tool name 'grep_files' is reserved for the built-in CALIBER tool
     'grep_files', which the protected-effect inventory classifies by name; register your tool under a
     different name", "status_code": 409}
```

The OpenAPI publish route answers the same `409`; recover by publishing the draft again with another `name` in the
request body. A tool draft Aria publishes under a reserved name is not registered: the draft ends as
`publish_failed` and the publish report carries `"success": false`, `"code": "reserved_tool_name"` and the same
message. Recover by asking Aria for a new tool draft under a different name and publishing that one.

A tool registered under a built-in's name **before** this rule is not migrated or rewritten. It is neutralised by
two things only: the identity check and an audit. A registry row counts as CALIBER's own only when every field the
seed writes matches (`workflows.builtin_tools.is_builtin_tool`): the name, the owner `@caliber`, the version `1.0`, a
callable named like the tool, and that tool's own module (`BUILTIN_TOOL_MODULE_BY_NAME`, which the seed also reads, so
the two cannot drift). `effects.inventory.effect_class_for_registry_tool` classifies every other row as
`irreversible_write`, the fail-closed class, and `tool_disposition_for_registry_tool` routes it through the dispatcher
instead of trusting it. The audit: every time the tool list seeds the built-ins, each row that holds a reserved name
without being the seed's own row is logged once per process at `ERROR` and gets one audit record (action
`flag_reserved_tool_name`, entity type `tool`, severity `high`, with `blocks_seed`). `blocks_seed: true` means the row is
at version `1.0` under the exact built-in name, so the registry (unique on name and version) cannot hold the real
built-in: it was never seeded and is missing from the list until the squatter is archived and renamed, or deleted
by an operator. To rename such a tool, register it again under a new name, point the workflows that use it at the new
name, then archive the old one (a registered tool cannot be renamed in place).

The owner is part of that identity, so `PATCH /tools/{id}` refuses (`409 reserved_tool_owner`) to give a registered
tool the owner `@caliber`, unless the row already matches the seed in every other field. That exception exists to repair
a built-in whose owner was edited away: until it is set back the row is untrusted (fail-closed) and the audit flags it;
a row that differs from the seed in name, version, module or callable can never be made trusted by editing its owner.

**Where trust comes from at run time.** The dispatch call sites (B07 #524, B08 #526, the B04 tasks) must pass the
registry row's own name, owner, module, callable and version, read from the database for the tool being run. They
must never pass a manifest binding's `local_name` or `resolved_name`, and `IRToolBinding` and `ToolRegistryEntry`
carry no owner on purpose: the IR is written into generated exports field by field, so an owner there would be data an
export author controls. A test fails when production code passes a constant or a `**kwargs` expansion to these
lookups.

**Refused until explicitly supported.** The inventory now marks two paths `refuse` for the reference profile, so
the dispatcher (B04.7, #774) will refuse them with `unsupported_in_reference_profile`:

| inventory row | path | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| EP-055 | the host-file tools `read_text_file`, `list_folder_files`, `grep_files`, `regex_search` | they read any host path, with no `confine_to_file_root`, and return what they read to the model provider (an `export`) |
| EP-114 | the write tools of the first-party PostgreSQL MCP server (`create_table`, `insert_rows`, `update_rows`, `delete_rows`, `execute_sql`, `create_vector_table`, `upsert_vectors`, `create_graph`, `drop_graph`, `create_vertex`, `create_edge`, `cypher_query`) | they create tables and write rows with no guard of their own; its read tools (`list_tables`, `describe_table`, `run_query`, `similarity_search`) run in a read-only transaction and are not refused |

`effects.inventory.tool_disposition(name, caliber_defined=...)` answers `refuse` or `dispatch` for a tool, on the same
trust rule as `effect_class`. The DB MCP write tools are not registry rows, so `tool_disposition_for_registry_tool`
answers `dispatch` for those names (a registry row is never the first-party server); their refusal rests on the MCP server's
identity, which the MCP route now establishes from the server record (`tool_disposition_for_mcp_tool`,
[Governed MCP tools](#governed-mcp-tools-b045)): a workflow tool node or MCP node reaching one of these tools on the first-party
server is refused with `unsupported_effect_path` **under the reference profile** (the development profile classifies it by the
administrator's policy; the first-party server is recognised from its stdio launch or an operator-attested managed sidecar host).
**The switch that raises `unsupported_in_reference_profile` for every refused row is #774**; the code-execution rows (`python_code`, `external_app` and an unsandboxed registered tool) raise it now ([Executable code is refused](#executable-code-is-refused-b124a-754)). The four host-file tools are already refused by a workflow `tool` node in a manifest-backed
plan (see "Governed registered tools"); until #774 lands, a model-chosen call of a host-file tool is refused only in a plan wired to the registry
(`build_plan`, the loop gate of [Model-selected tool calls](#model-selected-tool-calls-b046-768): `unsupported_effect_path`) and still
runs in the development profile and in a caller-built plan or export, so do not wire the four host-file tools into a reference workflow. The first-party database server's write tools are
refused through a workflow under the reference profile (B04.5), but a deployment that does not need the server should still not
register it.

**Configuration, migration and rollback.** No new setting, no migration and no stored data change. Rolling back is
reverting the change; rows already refused were never written.

## Executable code is refused (B12.4a, #754)

A workflow can run code in two ways, and the reference profile refuses both unless the platform itself puts the code behind
the sandbox it trusts. The kinds are read from the compiler's own IR kind registry (`caliber.workflows.ir.NodeType`), not from
a list kept by hand: each kind is classified once in `caliber.workflows.code_policy` (code, tool carrier or inert), and
`tests/test_profile_code_refusal.py` fails when a kind is added to the registry without being classified. Until it is, the kind is **refused**: the profile admits a kind only when it is classified as inert or as a tool carrier (fail closed).

| form | in the reference profile | why |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `python_code` node | refused | runs the author's Python source. The tool sandbox it runs in is a process boundary (separate interpreter, empty environment, rlimits) with ambient filesystem and network authority, not a container, VM or seccomp boundary. **A sandbox label does not establish isolation.** |
| `external_app` node | refused | imports and calls installed Python inside the control-plane process (EP-012) |
| registered `python_callable` tool, sandbox on (the default) | admitted | administrator-registered code run in the sandbox child: trusted-code admission, not containment of hostile code (the module allowlist is #763) |
| registered `python_callable` tool, `CALIBER_REGISTERED_TOOL_SANDBOX_ENABLED=false` | refused | the tool would be imported into the control plane (EP-015, EP-016, EP-019) |
| tool with any other execution backend | refused | the profile cannot establish that it runs no code (fail closed) |
| `openapi_http` tool, MCP tool binding | not code | an HTTP call the effect dispatcher governs, and an MCP call (no MCP server is allowlisted in the profile, #746) |

**One code, four boundaries.** Every refusal carries `unsupported_in_reference_profile`, the code ADR 0001 names for a refused path:

| boundary | what happens | where you see it |
| --- | --- | --- |
| validation (`POST /workflow-versions/{id}/validate`, and the validation inside compile and publish) | an error issue per node or tool, `path` `nodes.<id>` or `nodes.<id>.tools.<tool>` | `data.errors[].code` |
| compile (`POST /workflow-versions/{id}/compile`, publish, a run's plan) | `CompileError`; the same issues in `report.errors` | `400` with `report.errors[].code`; publish answers `400` with the code in `detail`; a run fails with `error_code` |
| promotion (promote, approve, rollback and every other alias move) | the alias does not move | `400` (promote) or `409` (approve) with the code in `detail` |
| runtime entry (`runtime.execute`, and the in-process tool binders) | the run ends `error` before any node runs, whatever built the plan | `WorkflowRunResult.error_code`, `error` starts with the code |

The runtime entry walks the whole IR, not only the nodes reachable from the start, so a dormant code node is refused too, and
a plan built by hand in a reference process (without `build_plan`) is refused by the process-wide policy that `create_app`
binds from the configuration. The in-process binders (`runtime._bind_in_process`, `bind_exported_tool`) refuse as a last
backstop. Nothing is written when a boundary refuses, and the node, the tool and the sandbox never run.

```text
POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/workflow-versions/WFV-6219b6e5/validate
200 {"data": {"valid": false, "errors": [{"code": "unsupported_in_reference_profile", "path": "nodes.code",
     "message": "python_code node 'code' runs author-supplied Python source in a sandbox that is a process boundary, not
     isolation (a sandbox label does not establish it); the reference profile does not support it, so remove the node or
     run this workflow outside the reference profile", "severity": "error"}], "warnings": []}}

POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/workflow-versions/WFV-6219b6e5/publish
400 {"detail": "version does not compile: unsupported_in_reference_profile: python_code node 'code' runs ..."}

POST /ajax-api/2.0/mlflow/caliber/workflows/WF-adb7d7f0/deployments/staging/promote   {"version_id": "WFV-6219b6e5"}
400 {"detail": "deployment preflight failed for alias 'staging': unsupported_in_reference_profile: python_code node 'code' runs ..."}
```

A run that was admitted before the code was refused ends `failed` with `error_code: unsupported_in_reference_profile` and the
node never executed. A registered Python tool with the sandbox switched off is refused at `nodes.<id>.tools.<tool>` with the
message `tool 'lookup_policy' runs registered Python (execution backend python_callable) and
CALIBER_REGISTERED_TOOL_SANDBOX_ENABLED is false, so it would run unsandboxed inside the control plane, ...`.

**Recovery.**

- A `python_code` or `external_app` node: remove it. Use a registered tool behind the sandbox, an OpenAPI tool or a built-in
  data-transform or template node for the same job, or author the workflow in a development deployment.
- An unsandboxed tool: set `CALIBER_REGISTERED_TOOL_SANDBOX_ENABLED=true` (the default) and restart the process.
- A version that was published before the profile was switched on and now holds code: it cannot be promoted or run. Author a
  new draft without the node and publish that; existing aliases keep pointing where they pointed, and are not rewritten.

**Configuration, migration and rollback.** No new setting, no migration and no stored data change. The development profile is
unchanged: all of these forms keep working there, and a version authored there is refused when a reference process validates,
compiles, promotes or runs it. The policy is process-wide state bound at startup (like the registered-tool module allowlist), so
a change of profile or sandbox setting needs a restart. Rolling back is reverting the change; nothing refused was written.

**What this does not do.** It does not decide which modules a registered tool may import (the module allowlist, #763), does not
contain hostile tool code (the sandbox is trusted-code admission, see "Who is trusted to write tools" in the tools guide), and
does not raise `unsupported_in_reference_profile` for the other `refuse` inventory rows (#774). A subworkflow node is not
expanded at the parent: the parent validates, compiles and promotes, and the child is checked at its own validation, compile,
promotion and runtime entry. A parent run over a child that holds code fails with the same code
(`error_code: unsupported_in_reference_profile`, `error` naming the child and the node) and the child's node never runs. The refinement, calibration and deploy-gate replays that build a plan without a configuration are covered by the
process-wide policy; in a reference deployment the app binds it at startup.

## Not enforced yet

ADR 0001 describes the whole reference shape; this table is what the *process* checks today. Not checked:

- **The shape itself:** one tenant and region, MLflow addressed by `MLFLOW_TRACKING_URI`, an S3-compatible object store, at least two projects, and one real model provider next to the scripted adapter. Readiness reporting for MLflow and the object store is #535. The PostgreSQL version and the `pgvector` extension are checked by the migrations (migration `0060`) and the migration-parity CI job, not by the profile.
- **Origin rules** (#533). ADR 0001 names them, but #533 has no allowed-origins task yet; that rule is not scheduled.
- **Run-time refusal of the other `refuse` inventory rows**, including the host-file tools and the DB MCP write tools (#774; see "Reserved tool names and refused paths"; code execution is refused since B12.4a, #754), **the trusted-connector set** (#534), **the full attack pack** (#535), **a single execution owner** (#536) and **the Apply separation-of-duties flag** (#589).
- **A governed effect context outside the worker's own graph** (#1051, #1068): the worker binds one for an admitted reference-profile run, but synchronous version runs, evaluation, gate and Aria previews, and the sub-workflows of a worker run have no owner lease and bind none, so the reference profile refuses their protected nodes (and an agent in them that can reach a mapped tool) and the development profile runs them on the legacy guarded path; see "Profiles and a missing governed context".
- **A verifier for the other workflow connectors** (#1055, #1051): a registered-tool, OpenAPI or MCP node, and a webhook or API-request node whose URL the operator did not list in `CALIBER_EFFECT_HTTP_VERIFIERS`, is refused `no_authoritative_verifier` in the reference profile because the connector has no lookup by key the platform can call; a governed agent step reaches `document_request` and a listed webhook reaches `http` end to end. A *permanent* unknown (a lookup that never shows the request) has no operator exit yet: the attested resolution is #1054. A workflow node whose effect ended unknown fails its run and a settlement does not resume it. Model-chosen calls of an agent that is not governed (B04.6, #768) are not routed.
- **Cookie flags:** `auth_session_cookie_secure` is not checked.
- **The database role:** whether the application connects as a role without `UPDATE`, `DELETE` or `TRUNCATE` on `caliber_run_manifests` (see "Run manifests are written once").

A configuration that passes this page is the minimum for the reference profile, not the whole of it.
